# Porting an xscreensaver hack

The rules live in `AGENTS.md` ("Rules", "Gotchas") and the path-scoped notes in
`.claude/rules/`. This skill sets the order of work and the points to stop. The
numbered steps are in `adding-a-hack.md` and the recipes it names are in
`techniques.md`, both next to this file. For several hacks in one go, read
`batches.md` too.

## 1. Pick, then read the source

Before copying anything, read `techniques.md` and every file in
`.claude/rules/` (`hacks.md`, `x11shim.md`, `device-display.md`, `gl.md`,
`tools-scoring.md`) in full. The gotchas live there, and a harness may not load
them for you (`.pi/rules` links to the same directory for pi).

Take S-rated rows from `docs/porting-assessment.md` first, and prefer a low
**Speed** band: the table runs each unported S hack on the host. The effort
rating counts missing shim calls, not memory, speed or stack (Braid was S, and
would have shown as high). A high band is a hack that will probably run slowly
on the board; a low band is not a guarantee, because a hack still doing
software `double` maths runs far slower on the device than on the host. Read
the hack's source before copying it, and look for:

| The source has | Technique (seen in) |
| --- | --- |
| Arrays or a state over a few MB | Build-time patch (Maze) |
| `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt`, `pow`, `double` in a hot loop | Single precision (Galaxy, Substrate) |
| Locals over a few KB | Stack check (Rorschach) |
| An allocation of 100 KB or more, or `exit()` on failure | Large allocations (Substrate) |
| Pixmaps, clip masks, a logo image | Images (Maze) |
| A hack that restarts itself | Restart leak test (Maze, Substrate) |
| A `free` that relies on state `draw` sets up (a lazy `initted`) | Stopping before the first draw (Blaster) |
| Hairlines, fades or `glPolygonOffset` in a GL hack | Thin lines in a GL hack |
| Xft text (`XftDrawStringUtf8`) | Xft text (XJack) |
| Threads, shared memory | Skipping a hack |
| A licence header | Read it; add a notices section only if it differs from jwz's |

## 2. Set up

Work in a worktree off `origin/main`. Its setup and the commands it refuses are
in "Worktree setup".

## 3. Red, copy, green

Follow `adding-a-hack.md`. Show the registry test failing before
copying. Fill each shim gap test-first, then break the code on purpose and
watch the test fail ("Tests that cannot be fooled"). Filling a missing
function is a shim gap. Changing what every hack sees (the runner, a default, a
shared helper) is not: stop and ask Rod first. A speed-up in the shared GL
layer counts too, even when every pinned frame hash still matches (HexTrail's
deferred depth clear): ask before writing it, and name it in the PR body.

## 4. Verify on the host

Run `pio test -e native`, `uv run --with pytest --with pillow pytest tools/tests`
and `uv run tools/check_notices.py`, and dump frames at several counts. For a
single-precision wrapper, also build for the device and run
`uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>`: a count in a per-frame function is
a literal, macro or struct the rename missed (`techniques.md`). Host
frames cannot show a byte swap, which happens in the push to the display: judge
colour on the device, on a colour you know the answer to.

## 5. Device

Flash only after Rod says so in this conversation; approval for one flash is
not approval for the next. See "Device capture". Report "compiles", "host tests
pass" and "runs on the device" separately; only Rod can say what the screen
shows. If it is slow, measure, change one thing, flash again and compare; if it
is still slow, say so and suggest dropping it. A hack that runs at a good rate
can still go: Rod dropped Boing (8.3 fps, "pretty boring on a small screen")
and asked for HexTrail to be tuned because it fell under 10 fps before the
rotation moved on. Judge a hack on a 466 px round screen, and by its worst
window as well as its mean. Record the numbers in
`tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, marking anything unmeasured as such. After a
batch, log one 20 s-a-hack rotation lap and run `tools/triage_hacks.py`
(`hacks.md` says how): it shows which hacks are step-bound, push-bound or paced
by their own delay, with their soft-double calls, so a slow hack is looked at
for the right reason.

## 6. Deliver

Commit named paths. Open the draft PR with `entire trail create` and put what
is unverified in its body. After a rebase, a push needs `--force-with-lease`:
ask Rod each time. Rod approves and merges; then delete the branch and
fast-forward `main`. New gotchas go in the matching `.claude/rules/` file (or
`AGENTS.md` if they apply everywhere) in the same PR, and deferred
ideas become issues.

## Done means

A port is done on the host only when all of these hold: a dumped frame viewed
at two or more frame counts (with seeds forced if the hack picks a mode); a
leak test, mutation-checked; the largest stack frame measured; the hash pinned
from a frame you looked at; and a notices row that matches each file's header.

## Red flags

| Thought | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| "It is rated S, so I need not read it" | Maze was rated L for Xlib gaps; the real blocker was a 20 MB `calloc`. |
| "It compiles, so it works" | Rorschach compiled and rebooted on its first frame. |
| "The colours look right" | Not from a host frame: every hack was byte swapped until Maze. |
| "My test passes, so it tests something" | A test through Pyro passed with the runner broken. Break the code on purpose. |
| "AGENTS.md says to fix shim gaps, so I can change the runner" | A new function is a gap. A change every hack sees needs Rod. |
| "Rod approved flashing earlier" | Ask again for each flash. |
| "Single precision is done, so the hack is as fast as it gets" | HexTrail gained 0.3 fps from it and 2.3 from a depth clear in the GL layer. Read what the shared code does each frame. |
| "The mean is above 10 fps" | HexTrail's mean was 15.3 and its worst window 10.8; its step grew all cycle. Read the lowest window. |
| "Dump with 0 and 5 frames exits cleanly, so it works" | That shows it starts and stops, not what it draws. Convert a frame to PNG and look. |
| "A `0` in `kBaseline` keeps the suite green" | It also stops the suite checking a single frame. Use `0x1ull` until you have looked, then pin. |
| "A hook will not run, so `--no-verify`" | That skips ruff, markdownlint and gitleaks. `SKIP=<hook>`, and say so in the PR. |

input.description: Inspect analogtv structure, precision and dependencies

content.text:
Rod, a quick update. I've read the port rules and Pong's source, and Linear has no ticket for it. AGENTS.md says to ask before starting work without one, so I'm stopping to ask.

**How hard is it? Moderate, with one big risk (speed).**

- **The code to copy:** `pong.c` is 1,108 lines of game logic. It draws everything through `analogtv`, xscreensaver's NTSC TV emulator. That means copying `analogtv.c` (2,459 lines) and `analogtv.h` unmodified.
- **What isn't ported yet:** nothing in the firmware uses `analogtv` today. Pong and `analogtv.c` need these shim gaps filled:
  - **Pointer and cursor calls:** `XGrabPointer`, `XUngrabPointer`, `XWarpPointer`, `XCreatePixmapCursor` and `XDefineCursor`.
  - **Screen and event names:** `XHeightMMOfScreen`, `XHeightOfScreen`, the event masks and `X11/keysym.h`.

  Most of these can be no-ops. The existing `xshm.h`, `thread_util.h` and `ximage.c` already cover the rest.
- **Memory:** `analogtv` holds a signal buffer of about 262 × 912 floats, roughly 1 MB. That goes in PSRAM, which has room.
- **Speed (the real risk):** each frame it synthesises and filters about 240,000 NTSC samples. It also mixes `double` and `float` maths, and the S3 has a single-precision FPU only. It then writes a window-sized image, and a full-frame PSRAM write costs about 25 ms. My guess, not a measurement, is 3–8 fps as copied.
- **Likely fixes:** a single-precision wrapper, a lower `ANALOGTV_SCALE`, no noise or ghosting, and a smaller render size via `lowrez_put.h`. If it stays under about 8 fps, the honest answer may be to drop it, as with Boing.

**Can I file a Linear ticket on ARS for the Pong port (labels `stopwatch-screensaver` plus a Work Type, a priority, status In Progress) and start on `feature/ARS-NN-pong`?** The first step would be the failing registry test, then the shim gaps, then a host dump to measure the step time.
Yes, let's go for it.

# Linear tracking

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

## Filing issues

- Every issue gets the `stopwatch-screensaver` label (in the `Repo` group) and exactly
  one label from the `Work Type` group. The group is single-select, so
  pick the one that fits best (see below).
- Always set a priority (Urgent, High, Medium, Low). Never leave it at
  "No priority".
- Link the draft trail or spec section if one exists. Copy the body from
  `entire trail show N --json`; `entire trail list --json` returns empty
  bodies.

## Choosing a Work Type

| Label         | Use it for                                       |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `Bug`         | Fixing something that isn't operating correctly. |
| `Feature`     | Adding new functionality to the app.             |
| `Enhancement` | Improving existing functionality.                |
| `Performance` | Improving the performance of code.               |
| `Chore`       | Maintenance, tooling and documentation work.     |

Several of these can fit one ticket. Decide by asking these in order and
taking the first yes:

1. Does the app do something other than what was intended? `Bug`, even if
   the symptom is slowness or the fix is a refactor.
1. Is the behaviour right, but too slow or heavy, and is speed or
   resource use the point of the work? `Performance`.
1. Does it give the user a capability they did not have? `Feature`.
1. Does it make a capability they already have better? `Enhancement`.
1. Does it change nothing a user would notice? `Chore`.

A ticket that bundles small, unrelated tidy-ups takes `Chore`. If the
bundle is mostly one other type, either split it or use that type.
Refactors, test additions, dependency bumps, build scripts, CI and
documentation are `Chore` unless they fix a defect.

## Status names

Use these exactly as Linear spells them: `Backlog`, `Todo`,
`In Progress`, `In Review`, `Done`, `Canceled`, `Duplicate`.
Port a new hack = `Feature`. Filing the ticket.

Shim gaps to fill: `XGrabPointer`, `XUngrabPointer`, `XWarpPointer`, `XCreatePixmapCursor`, `XDefineCursor`, `XHeightMMOfScreen`, `XHeightOfScreen`, the event masks and `X11/keysym.h`.

# Working in a git worktree

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- In a git worktree the ignored `vendor/`, `.venv/` and `.platformio/` are
  missing. Symlink them from the main checkout. `.gitignore`'s trailing slashes
  don't match symlinks, so they would show as untracked, but the shared
  `.git/info/exclude` already lists the three names. That file is shared by
  every worktree: ask Rod before adding to it.
  The harness refuses `source tools/env.sh` and a computed `PATH` there: run
  `PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<worktree>/.platformio ../.venv/bin/pio ...` instead,
  and keep commands plain (no scripts, loops, `$VAR` in a command or `&&`
  chains with a computed path). A worktree an agent works in (`isolation:
  "worktree"`) starts from `origin/main`, not from your branch, and has no
  vendor or toolchain until you link them.
  It also refuses heredocs, `git -C` and `cd` into another worktree: use the
  Edit and Write tools. It refuses `git ... | tar` and `cd <dir> && git ...`
  too: use `git archive -o f.tar <sha>` then `tar -x -f f.tar -C <dir>`, and run
  git from the worktree root. A background shell starts there as well, so use
  `pio test -d <abs>/firmware` with absolute paths. Parallel calls can race
  (a `uv run` in the root disturbed `.venv` while `pio` ran:
  "../.venv/bin/pio: no such file"), so run
  `uv` and `pio` one at a time. To fast-forward `main` or remove the worktree,
  leave it first with `ExitWorktree keep`. If no checkout has `main` out,
  `git fetch origin main:main` fast-forwards it from anywhere.
  Before `ExitWorktree remove` on a merged branch, check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main`; the tool's "discarded N
  commits" count ignores merges. `.platformio`, `.venv` and `vendor` there are
  symlinks, so removal leaves the real ones alone. After a merge,
  `ExitWorktree keep` names a branch (`worktree-<name>`) that may not exist:
  remove the worktree with `git worktree remove --force <path>` and delete the
  real branch, as separate commands, because a failed `&&` link skips the rest
  silently. Check `git worktree list` afterwards. `git worktree remove --force`
  fails on a worktree this session's harness locked ("cannot remove a locked
  working tree, lock reason: claude session"): once the tip is an ancestor of
  `origin/main`, `ExitWorktree remove` with `discard_changes: true` works, and
  its "discarded N commits" are the merged ones. In a session resumed from a
  summary, `ExitWorktree` can be a no-op ("no active EnterWorktree session"):
  remove the worktree with `git worktree remove --force <path>` from the main
  checkout instead. To delete the merged branch
  you are standing on, `git switch --detach origin/main` in the worktree first.
  The shell's directory resets after each command and after `ExitWorktree`, so
  use absolute paths (`../.venv/bin/pio` failed from the wrong place and the run
  looked like a test failure). A loop over several mutations is refused as a
  command: write it as a script in the scratchpad that edits the file, runs
  `pio test` through `subprocess` and restores the file in `finally`, then run
  it with `python3 -I`.
  Stopping such a script (TaskStop) kills it before `finally` runs: check
  `git diff` afterwards and restore the file by hand.
  Also refused: a heredoc (use the Write tool for a scratchpad script), `$(...)`
  inside a git command, and the quoted `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` above combined
  with a redirect or `NO_COLOR=1`. Flashing worked as
  `PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<wt>/.platformio PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="..."
  .venv/bin/pio run -d firmware -e stopwatch -t upload` with no redirect: the
  540 KB of output lands in a tool-results file, so grep that for "Hash of data
  verified". Edit and Write refuse the main checkout's path while you are in a
  worktree. `pio test -f test_x` runs the whole suite (`test_hacks` takes 3
  minutes, the full native run 7), and a failing summary reads "2 failed, 101
  succeeded": match `[FAILED]` or the return code, not "succeeded".
- `uv run ty check` (the pre-commit `ty` hook) fails in a worktree with
  "Failed to spawn: ty": the shared `.venv` has no `ty`. Run
  `uvx ty check --python .venv` instead (it passes on a clean tree), then
  commit with `SKIP=ty git commit ...`, and say in the PR that the hook was
  skipped. `ruff-format` rewrites a file and aborts the commit when a line is
  too long: restage the file and commit again.
- Also refused in a worktree session: a shell variable used as a program's
  argument (`S=...; prog $S/x`), a `for` loop that runs `uv` or `pio`, and
  `entire trail finding resolve -m "..."` text containing `*` or backticks.
  Spell out absolute paths, run one command per call, and keep `-m` text to
  plain words.

    reg = _insert_before(reg, "const HackEntry *const g_hacks[]", decl + "\n")
    g = _guard_in(reg, "g_hacks[] = {", "};")
    if g >= 0:
        reg = reg[:g] + f"    &{name}_hack,\n" + reg[g:]
    else:
        reg, n = re.subn(
            r"    &(\w+)_hack\};", rf"    &\1_hack,\n    &{name}_hack}};", reg, count=1
        )
        if n != 1:

    t = tests.read_text()
    g = _guard_in(t, "expected[] = {", "const int n = sizeof(expected)")
    if g >= 0:

    else:
        t, n = re.subn(
            r'"\};\n  const int n = sizeof\(expected\)',
            f'",\n                                         "{cls}"}};\n  const int n = sizeof(expected)',
            t,
            count=1,
        )
        if n != 1:

    g = _guard_in(

    )
    if g >= 0:
        t = t[:g] + f"    0, /* {cls}: not yet pinned */\n" + t[g:]

    leak = (

"""Mutation check for the Pong shim gaps and wrapper. Run with python3 -I."""

import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

WT = Path("/Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/worktrees/pong")
FW = WT / "firmware"
PIO = WT / ".venv" / "bin" / "pio"
ENV = {
    "PATH": "/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin:/opt/homebrew/bin",
    "HOME": "/Users/rod",
    "PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR": str(WT / ".platformio"),
    "NO_COLOR": "1",
}

MUTANTS = [
    ("wrapper: no swap of red", "firmware/src/hacks/pong_tv.c",
     "it->red_values[i] = px_swap((uint16_t)it->red_values[i]);",
     "it->red_values[i] = (uint16_t)it->red_values[i];", "test_pong_wrapper"),
    ("wrapper: no swap of green", "firmware/src/hacks/pong_tv.c",
     "it->green_values[i] = px_swap((uint16_t)it->green_values[i]);",
     "it->green_values[i] = (uint16_t)it->green_values[i];", "test_pong_wrapper"),
    ("wrapper: no swap of blue", "firmware/src/hacks/pong_tv.c",
     "it->blue_values[i] = px_swap((uint16_t)it->blue_values[i]);",
     "it->blue_values[i] = (uint16_t)it->blue_values[i];", "test_pong_wrapper"),
    ("wrapper: swap only when use_cmap", "firmware/src/hacks/pong_tv.c",
     "if (it && !it->use_cmap) {", "if (it && it->use_cmap) {", "test_pong_wrapper"),
    ("shim: screen height wrong", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshim.c",
     "return g_current_display ? g_current_display->canvas->h : 0;",
     "return g_current_display ? g_current_display->canvas->w + 1 : 0;", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: panel height wrong", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshim.h",
     "#define XHeightMMOfScreen(screen) ((void)(screen), 44)",
     "#define XHeightMMOfScreen(screen) ((void)(screen), 45)", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: grab fails", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshim.c",
     "(void)keyboard_mode, (void)confine_to, (void)cursor, (void)time;\n  return GrabSuccess;",
     "(void)keyboard_mode, (void)confine_to, (void)cursor, (void)time;\n  return 1;", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: visual not true colour", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshm.c",
     "  return TrueColor;", "  return PseudoColor;", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: red mask wrong", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshm.c",
     "*red_mask = 0xF800;", "*red_mask = 0x7C00;", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: green mask wrong", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshm.c",
     "*green_mask = 0x07E0;", "*green_mask = 0x03E0;", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: thread_malloc never fails but returns nothing", "firmware/src/x11shim/thread_util.c",
     "*ptr = malloc(size);", "*ptr = calloc(1, 1);", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: XQueryColors does only the first", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshim.c",
     "for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) XQueryColor(dpy, cmap, &colors[i]);",
     "for (int i = 0; i < 1 && i < n; i++) XQueryColor(dpy, cmap, &colors[i]);", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: format not recorded", "firmware/src/x11shim/ximage.c",
     "  im->format = format;\n", "", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: XYPixmap refused", "firmware/src/x11shim/ximage.c",
     "(format == XYBitmap || format == XYPixmap) && depth == 1",
     "format == XYBitmap && depth == 1", "test_xshim"),
    ("shim: FocusChangeMask wrong", "firmware/src/x11shim/xshim.h",
     "#define FocusChangeMask (1L << 21)", "#define FocusChangeMask (1L << 20)", "test_xshim"),
]


def run(test: str) -> tuple[int, str]:
    p = subprocess.run(
        [str(PIO), "test", "-e", "native", "-f", test],
        cwd=FW, env=ENV, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=900,
    )
    out = p.stdout + p.stderr
    summary = [l for l in out.splitlines() if "test cases" in l]
    return p.returncode, (summary[-1] if summary else "no summary")


def main() -> int:
    for t in ("test_pong_wrapper", "test_xshim"):
        rc, s = run(t)
        print(f"BASELINE {t}: rc={rc} {s}", flush=True)
        if rc != 0:
            print("baseline fails: stopping")
            return 1
    survived = []
    for name, rel, old, new, test in MUTANTS:
        path = WT / rel
        original = path.read_text()
        assert original.count(old) == 1, (name, original.count(old))
        try:
            path.write_text(original.replace(old, new))
            assert path.read_text() != original
            rc, s = run(test)
        finally:
            path.write_text(original)
        verdict = "killed" if rc != 0 else "SURVIVED"
        if rc == 0:
            survived.append(name)
        print(f"{verdict}: {name} ({test}: {s})", flush=True)
    print("survivors:", survived)
    return 0


sys.exit(main())

Rod, Pong is ported on the host and committed as WIP (789ec6b on `feature/ARS-59-pong`). I need your go-ahead to flash, because speed and stack can only be measured on the board.

**What's done and checked**
- **Source:** the copies of `pong.c`, `analogtv.c` and `analogtv.h` are byte-identical to upstream (`cmp`), and `check_notices.py` passes.
- **Build:** they build as one unit through `hacks/pong_tv.c`. The wrapper swaps analogtv's colour tables once, so pixels come out in canvas byte order with no per-pixel cost.
- **Shim gaps filled test-first:**
  - **Pointer, cursor and focus:** no-ops for `XGrabPointer`, `XWarpPointer`, `XDefineCursor` and friends.
  - **Visual and screen:** screen height, `visual_class`, and RGB565 masks.
  - **Memory and colours:** `thread_malloc`, `XQueryColors`, `XImage.format`, one-bit `XYPixmap` images, and a few compatibility headers.
- **Tests:**

  - **`test_xshim`:** 314 of 314 pass.
  - **`test_hacks`:** 150 of 150 pass, including the leak test and the stop-before-first-frame test.
  - **Pong wrapper test:** 2 of 2 pass.
- **Builds:** the dump build and the device build both compile and link.
- **Frames:** I viewed frames at 200 and 1500 on the host. It's authentic Pong with scores, ball, paddles, NTSC noise and ghosting.

**Not yet established**
- **Speed:** the host step is 3.6 ms, which isn't a guide to the S3. My estimate is 5–8 fps, which is a guess.
- **Stack:** the line loop frame is 9,328 bytes and the filter's is 3,264 bytes, about 12.6 KB of the 16 KB before the runner's frames. If it's too tight, I'd patch the 9 KB array to the heap at build time, keeping the copy byte-identical.
- **Pin:** the frame hash isn't pinned yet (`0` in `kBaseline`). I'll pin after any speed or stack changes, so the hash isn't taken twice.
- **Bezel:** paddles and scores sit near the edges, so the round bezel clips the corners. An inscribed-square render would fix it but costs resolution, so it's your call after you've seen it.

**Request:** may I flash a Pong-pinned build (`-DSTART_HACK="pong" -DROTATE_SECONDS=0`) with a temporary stack high-water log, and capture about 150 s of serial? That gives fps, step, push, heap and stack. I'll send the output to a file and check "Hash of data verified". Serial port is `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` unless you've moved the board.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/skills/device-run

# Flashing and measuring on the device

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `pio run -e stopwatch`: build for the device. Add `-t upload` to flash.
  The device starts on a random hack; to pin one while examining it, prefix
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS='-DSTART_HACK=\"galaxy\"'` (a name from `g_hacks[]`,
  any case; an unknown name falls back to random and logs it). Rebuild without
  it afterwards, since the define sticks to the build. Unescaped quotes fail
  with "error: 'truchet' was not declared in this scope".
  It rotates to the next hack every 90 s (a button press restarts the count);
  `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5` shortens that for leak testing and `=0` turns it off. A
  pinned build still rotates, so add `=0` to measure one hack.
  The log prints `rotate -> <hack> heap= psram=` at each change. Combine flags
  in one `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` string.
  `-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod\ B.\"` sets the name badge text (default "Rod" over
  "Begbie"; `\n` starts a new line). Check a
  flag reached the binary with
  `strings -a -n 3 .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c '^Rod B\.$'`:
  plain `strings` skips anything under 4 characters.
  `-DQR_URL=\"https://example.com\"` sets the QR overlay's target (default the
  LinkedIn profile). Check it reached the binary with
  `strings -a .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c 'example.com'`.
  In a worktree session the harness refuses backslash-escaped flag values and
  `$(cat file)`. Use `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="'-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod B.\"'
  '-DSTART_HACK=\"gears\"' -DROTATE_SECONDS=0"` with `.venv/bin/pio run -d
  firmware -e stopwatch -t upload` from the worktree root.
- Serial log: `.venv/bin/python -I tools/serial_capture.py <out-file>
  <seconds> [port]` reads `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` at 115200 into a file and
  reopens the port when it goes away. Run it in the background with absolute
  paths, since background shells ignore `cd`. Lines to read:
  `run <hack> fps= step= push= sync= wait= rows=` (ms per frame in the hack,
  the push, the wait for the panel's TE edge before a synced push (only
  Unknown Pleasures; not counted in `push=`) and the wait; mean canvas rows
  sent per frame, 466 being a full push,
  though overlay redraws made while waiting can push it higher)
  and `switch -> <hack> press_waited=`. An empty capture, or "Device not
  configured", means the USB port went away and came back (a flash, a crash):
  reopen it in a loop. Opening the port resets the board
  (`rst:0x15 USB_UART_CHIP_RESET`, even with DTR/RTS held low): the overlay
  returns to nothing and a random hack starts. To measure one hack, flash a
  pinned build (`START_HACK` plus `ROTATE_SECONDS=0`), start the capture, then
  tap during it: the early windows are the baseline, the later ones have the
  overlay.
  `serial_capture.py` sets `dtr` and `rts` to False on an unopened
  `serial.Serial()` before `open()`, as any script of your own must: a reopen
  loop without that once parked the chip in its bootloader
  (`boot:0x3 ... waiting for download`, screen frozen). Recover, or reset just
  before a capture to log from boot (a hack's `fprintf(stderr)` reaches the
  log), with `.venv/bin/python .platformio/packages/tool-esptoolpy/esptool.py
  --chip esp32s3 --port /dev/cu.usbmodem112401 --after hard_reset read_mac`.
- Flash with `pio run -e stopwatch -t upload > file 2>&1`, never piped through
  `head`, and check for "Hash of data verified". The button steps backwards
  (Pyro, then Lightning, then Drift...). Work out how long a restart takes
  from the hack's cycle count times its frame time (Substrate: 10,000 cycles
  at about 160 ms is 27 minutes) and capture that long, with rotation off.
- `ad-flyingtoasters` force flags (add to `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS`):
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_ART=0|1` (0 is 1-bit, 1 is colour) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_DONENESS=0|1|2` (light, medium, dark) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_SCALE=1|2` (2 is the default, with 6 flyers; 1 is the
  original size, with 10); a number outside those is an `#error`. It logs
  `ad-flyingtoasters: <art>, doneness=<level>` to stderr at start.
- To see where a GL hack's frame goes, add `-DGL_PROFILE`: a `glprof` line
  follows each `run` line with time per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill). Time left
  over is the hack's own code. To compare builds, `.venv/bin/python -I
  tools/ab_flash.py --hack Gears --seconds 60 --rounds 2 --out <dir>
  "a=-DGL_PROFILE" "b=-DGL_PROFILE -DFOO"` builds each variant pinned, flashes
  them in turn and tabulates the windows. It flashes: run it only with Rod's
  go-ahead. It builds each hack's variants from the working tree when that
  hack's turn starts, so leave `src/` and `tools/tinygl_patch.py` alone until
  the last hack has built. It compares flag variants of one tree: to A/B a
  change, put it behind a temporary `-D` switch (as `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` does).
  It takes one `--hack` per run: loop several from a scratchpad script run
  with `run_in_background`, and `touch` a done file at the end.
- `-DDCACHE_LINE32` keeps the SDK's 32-byte data-cache lines for every hack
  (the default is 64 bytes, see `device-display.md`), so it is the A side of an
  `ab_flash` comparison. `-DPSRAM_BENCH` boots into `diag/psram_bench.h`
  instead of the runner and prints cost per cache miss, sequential rates and a
  working-set sweep; `-DPSRAM_BENCH_VARIANT=0..3` picks the line size and
  prefetch setting.
- `esptool` reads of the 16 MB flash need `--baud 921600` (about 3.5 minutes)
  and show no progress when piped.
- The port name changes with the USB socket the board is plugged into
  (`/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` became `/dev/cu.usbmodem101` on 2026-10-14). When
  it is missing, find the board without touching it:
  `ioreg -p IOUSB -l -w0 | grep -E "\+-o|idVendor|idProduct|USB Product
  Name|USB Serial Number"` lists USB devices, and
  `ioreg -r -c IOSerialBSDClient -l | grep IOCalloutDevice` lists the serial
  ports. The StopWatch is the "USB JTAG/serial debug unit" from Espressif
  (`idVendor` 12346, `idProduct` 4097). Its USB serial number is its MAC:
  Rod's board is `28:84:85:43:B2:70`, so check that before flashing a port
  you have not used before. Pass `--upload-port <port>` to `pio run -t upload`
  and read the same port for the serial log, and leave `platformio.ini`'s
  `upload_port` alone. Still ask Rod before each flash. The auto-mode
  classifier refused a flash to an overridden port once: give Rod the command
  to run with `!`.
- Another session may be using the board. Before flashing, run `lsof
  /dev/cu.usbmodem112401`: a "multiple access on port" upload error was
  another session's serial capture, and esptool's connect resets the board
  under it. Ask Rod before flashing over someone else's run.
- PlatformIO cleans the build directory, image and all, when
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` changes: an `-t nobuild -t upload` with other flags
  finds no `firmware.bin`. To keep several images, give each its own
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_DIR` (the build scripts all use `$BUILD_DIR`).
- Read `push=` from a hack's second 5 s window on: the name overlay is stamped
  inside the push timing while it shows, so the first window reads high.
- `heap=` and `psram=` are the reading at the end of a window, not a minimum:
  a hack with a long pause and nothing held in it (Celtic's 5 s `*delay2`)
  reads idle in every window. Sample while it works, or read `rotate ->`.
- Report a hack's lowest `fps=` window as well as its mean. HexTrail's step
  grows over a 65 s cycle: mean 15.3, worst window 10.8, and Rod saw an earlier
  build sag under 10 fps before the rotation moved on. Capture a full cycle and
  say which build the board holds when you stop.
- A boot is deterministic (same hack, layout and windows), so to compare two
  builds flash them alternately and compare window by window; one reading in
  three captures was an unexplained outlier, so never trust a single pair.
- Leak-testing with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5`: internal heap falls about 26 KB
  during the first lap and then stays flat. Compare lap 2 with lap 3, not
  with lap 1. PSRAM should match exactly on every visit.
- To prove a device-only path the host cannot run (the ROM's `tinfl`), add a
  temporary `#ifdef` block after `printStats("boot")` in `main.cpp` that logs
  a checksum, compare it with one computed in Python, then `git checkout
  firmware/src/main.cpp` before pushing.
Checking the board is where it should be and nothing else holds the port, then I'll look at where the stats line is printed to add the temporary stack high-water.

Rod, Pong runs on the board but at 2.8 fps as copied. I'm stopping here to check the plan with you, because that's far below the 5–8 fps I guessed.

**What the board showed**
- **Speed:** 2.8 fps (2.6 in the first window), flat over 150 s. Step is 356 ms and push 24.8 ms, so the step is 93% of the frame.
- **Stability:** no canary, no reboot. Heap and PSRAM stayed flat.
- **Stack:** the high-water mark left 2,788 bytes free of 16 KB, so Pong uses about 13.6 KB. It's safe but with a thin margin. A heap patch for the 9 KB array stays an option if we keep it.
- **Flash:** 61.6% of the app partition.
- **State of the board and tree:** the board holds the pinned Pong build, with the temporary stack log inside it. I reverted that log in the tree (`git checkout main.cpp`). The WIP commit 789ec6b is unchanged.

**Why it's slow (my reasoning, not measured)**
- **Whole signal, every frame:** `analogtv` synthesises about 239,000 NTSC samples into a 955 KB float buffer in PSRAM, whatever Pong draws. It then filters 200 lines and renders 466 × 466 pixels.
- **Memory passes:** by my estimate that is about 150 ms of PSRAM passes (noise write, add, subtotals, read-back, image write, copy to canvas) on top of about 175 ms of float maths.
- **Wasted work:** nearly all of it repeats a picture that barely changes.

**Why it matters for Pong:** the game is paced per frame at about 30 fps upstream. At 2.8 fps the ball jumps about 6 px or more a frame, so it would look like slow motion with big jumps, not a game.

1. **Split the step on the device.** I'd flash three temporary variants (skip the noise pass, skip the line loop, skip the put) through `ab_flash` to see which stage dominates before touching anything. About 15 minutes and three more flashes, which I'd need you to approve.
2. **Cut resolution and work.** Render the TV at the 266 × 200 minimum and scale up (`lowrez_put.h` style). A build-time patch could also limit the signal passes to the lines Pong draws. This risks the NTSC look and needs a byte-identity-preserving patch.
3. **Drop it.** Record it in `tools/failed_ports.txt` with the 2.8 fps number, as with Boing. It keeps the shim gaps, `analogtv`, and the `pong_tv.c` and notices work for the other analogtv hacks (xanalogtv, apple2, and others).

"""Build-time patch for analogtv: the ghost filter in float.

analogtv_add_signal adds every sample of the picture to the receiver's buffer
and mixes in a ghost from the four taps in `rec->ghostfir`, which the struct
holds as `double`. Each group of four samples therefore multiplies four floats
by doubles and adds them (seven software double operations plus the
conversions, since the ESP32-S3's FPU is single precision only), about 175
cycles a sample over the 238,944 samples of a frame. On the board that was
209 of Pong's 356 ms step: with the signal passes skipped it dropped to 146 ms.

The copied analogtv.c stays byte-identical to upstream. The firmware build runs
this on its text (firmware/patch_analogtv.py) and the wrapper
src/hacks/pong_tv.c includes the result. The taps are read once per call into
floats; their sum is then a float, so the loop does float maths only. Results
differ from the double loop only in the last bits of a float, which the test
checks against the real function at levels from 0.001 to 10,000.

The replacements are checked, so a change upstream fails the build loudly.
"""

OLD_TAPS = "  float hfloss=rec->hfloss;\n"

NEW_TAPS = """\
  float hfloss=rec->hfloss;
  float ghostfir0=rec->ghostfir[0], ghostfir1=rec->ghostfir[1];
  float ghostfir2=rec->ghostfir[2], ghostfir3=rec->ghostfir[3];
"""

OLD_SUM = """\
    sigr=(dp[1]*rec->ghostfir[0] + dp[2]*rec->ghostfir[1] +
          dp[3]*rec->ghostfir[2] + dp[4]*rec->ghostfir[3]);
"""

NEW_SUM = """\
    sigr=(dp[1]*ghostfir0 + dp[2]*ghostfir1 +
          dp[3]*ghostfir2 + dp[4]*ghostfir3);
"""


def _replace_once(source: str, old: str, new: str) -> str:
    found = source.count(old)
    if found != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"expected 1 of `{old.strip()[:40]}...` in analogtv.c, found {found}; "
            "has upstream changed?"
        )
    return source.replace(old, new)


def float_ghost_filter(source: str) -> str:
    source = _replace_once(source, OLD_TAPS, NEW_TAPS)
    return _replace_once(source, OLD_SUM, NEW_SUM)

"""Compare two raw RGB565 frames: pixels that differ, and by how much per channel."""

import sys
from pathlib import Path

a = Path(sys.argv[1]).read_bytes()
b = Path(sys.argv[2]).read_bytes()
assert len(a) == len(b), (len(a), len(b))
n = len(a) // 2
diff = 0
worst = 0
total = 0
for i in range(n):
    pa = a[2 * i] | (a[2 * i + 1] << 8)
    pb = b[2 * i] | (b[2 * i + 1] << 8)
    if pa != pb:
        diff += 1
        ch = max(
            abs((pa >> 11) - (pb >> 11)),
            abs(((pa >> 5) & 63) - ((pb >> 5) & 63)) // 2,
            abs((pa & 31) - (pb & 31)),
        )
        worst = max(worst, ch)
        total += ch
print(f"{sys.argv[1].split('/')[-1]}: {diff} of {n} pixels differ, worst channel step {worst}, mean {total / max(diff, 1):.2f}")

Rod, found it and fixed it on the host. The fix is committed as 8a706c7 and not yet on the board.

**What the five-variant run showed** (one 45 s window each, as copied, flashed one after another):

| Variant | step | Stage cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| base | 355.9 ms (2.8 fps) | |
| skip noise and signal passes | 146.5 ms | **209 ms** |
| skip line loop | 235.2 ms | 121 ms |
| skip put | 341.9 ms | 14 ms |
| skip all three | 13.0 ms | the floor |

**Cause of the 209 ms:** `analogtv_add_signal` multiplies each float sample by `rec->ghostfir[]`, which are `double` fields. On the S3 that is seven software-double operations plus conversions per group of four samples, about 175 cycles a sample across 238,944 samples a frame. The same stage in float should be about 30 ms.

**The fix:** a build-time patch (`tools/analogtv_patch.py`, run by `firmware/patch_analogtv.py`) reads the four taps once as floats. `analogtv.c` and `pong.c` stay byte-identical.
- **Tests:** 6 patch tests, and 6 of 6 patch mutants killed. One test compiles the real `analogtv_add_signal` before and after and compares it at levels from 0.001 to 10,000, within 1e-4 relative error. The full Python suite passes (680 passed, 1 skipped).
- **Frames:** host frames are byte-identical to the unpatched ones at frame counts 5, 200 and 1500.

**My prediction, before measuring:** step about 170–200 ms and about 5 fps (hand arithmetic: 13 floor + about 35 signal + 121 lines + 14 put). That is still well short of the 10 fps bar. The line loop (121 ms: three IIR filters per sample plus PSRAM misses) is then the next target.

**Request:** may I flash the patched build, pinned, for a 150 s capture to check the prediction? If it lands near 5 fps, the options after that are:
1. Reduce resolution or signal work (patch the line loop).
2. Accept about 5 fps and tune the ball speed so the game still reads as Pong.
3. Drop it, as with Boing.
Yes, flash the patched build.

import subprocess

    ("patch: loop ignores the step", PATCH,
     "lineno += it->threads.count * pong_line_step) {\n\"\"\"\n\nOLD_GET_LINE",
     "lineno += it->threads.count) {\n\"\"\"\n\nOLD_GET_LINE"),
    ("patch: covers only one skipped line", PATCH,
     "for (k = 1; k < pong_line_step && lineno + k < ANALOGTV_BOT; k++) {",
     "for (k = 1; k < 2 && lineno + k < ANALOGTV_BOT; k++) {"),
    ("patch: counts nothing", PATCH, "    pong_lines_drawn++;\n", "    \n"),
    ("patch: walks past the last line", PATCH,
     "k < pong_line_step && lineno + k < ANALOGTV_BOT; k++", "k < pong_line_step; k++"),
    ("wrapper: view not centred horizontally", WRAP,
     "pong_view_xo = (a->width - pong_view_size) / 2;", "pong_view_xo = 0;"),
    ("wrapper: view not centred vertically", WRAP,
     "pong_view_yo = (a->height - pong_view_size) / 2;", "pong_view_yo = 0;"),
    ("wrapper: view size ignored", WRAP,
     "if (pong_view_size > 0 && pong_view_size < a->width && pong_view_size < a->height) {",
     "if (0) {"),
    ("wrapper: put ignores the view offset", WRAP,

    ("wrapper: put ignores the vertical offset", WRAP,

    ("wrapper: always overlaps", WRAP, "pong_overrides, 0, 0, PONG_VIEW == 0};",
     "pong_overrides, 0, 0, 1};"),
]


def run(test: str) -> tuple[int, str]:

    )
    out = p.stdout + p.stderr
    summary = [l for l in out.splitlines() if "test cases" in l]
    return p.returncode, (summary[-1] if summary else "no summary")


def main() -> int:
    rc, s = run("test_pong_wrapper")

**Fixed since last time:**
- **First line-step attempt:** it drew dark bands across the picture. I had made each stepped line one tall line, but analogtv builds its scanline shading table only for row heights near the average (2–3 rows), so the taller lines picked up empty entries and came out black. A new test catches it (330 black rows at step 2, none at step 1).
- **The fix:** each stepped line's colours are now written into the skipped line's rows at that line's own height. Frames now look right, with solid paddles, the net's dashes and the score digits.

- **Line step:** every Nth line is drawn (default 2).
- **330 px view:** an optional centred view inside the round glass, which fixes the bezel clipping. I measured its look on the host only.
- **Overlap flag:** Pong is flagged `repaints_all` in the default whole-window build.
- **Noise:** dialled back from 0.04 to 0.02.

**Next:**
1. When the suite finishes I'll commit.
2. Then I'll ask you for the flash. I'd run `ab_flash` with four variants, about 15 minutes, to see what 1 and 3 get us:
   - whole window, step 1, overlap (item 1 alone)

   I expect roughly 5, 7, 7 and 5 fps, but that's a guess until measured.

Rod, the measurements are in, and they mostly landed on my predictions (45 s each, 7 windows, no canary or reboot in any variant).

| Variant | fps | step | push | rows | My prediction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| before (previous flash) | 4.6 | 194.6 ms | 24.8 ms | 466 | |
| **a**: whole window, step 1, overlap (item 1 alone), upstream noise | 5.0 | 201.9 ms | hidden | 466 | about 5 |
| **b**: whole window, step 2, overlap, noise 0.02 | 6.4 | 155.2 ms | hidden | 466 | about 7 |
| **c**: 330 px view, step 2, no overlap | **7.2** | 124.2 ms | 15.1 ms | 330 | about 7 |
| **d**: 330 px view, step 1, no overlap | 5.6 | 163.9 ms | 15.1 ms | 330 | about 5 |

**What each lever bought**
- **Overlap (item 1):** 4.6 to 5.0 fps (+8.7%). The push drops out of the frame, but the step grows 7 ms from cache contention, as for the other overlapped hacks.
- **Line step 2:** takes 47 ms off the step on the whole window (201.9 to 155.2) and 40 ms on the 330 view (163.9 to 124.2).
- **330 px view:** about 38 ms off the step (201.9 to 163.9), at the cost of the overlap. It also fixes the bezel clipping.
- **Best result, c:** the 330 px view with step 2 gives 7.2 fps, up from 4.6 (1.57×), with nothing cut by the bezel. A 139 ms frame is 124 ms of step plus 15 ms of push.

It's still under the 10 fps bar. The board now holds `d` (330 px view, step 1), because `ab_flash` leaves the last variant on it.

**Where the remaining 124 ms in `c` probably goes** (my arithmetic from the earlier stage split, not measured at this setting): about 45 ms of noise and signal passes, about 40 ms of line loop, about 13 ms of floor, and about 7 ms of put. The signal passes are the biggest chunk left, and neither the line step nor the view shrinks them.

**Your call on next steps**
1. **Step 3 on the 330 px view.** The line loop is a third of the work, so I'd guess about 100 ms, or 8.5 fps. The cost is vertical resolution: 67 drawn lines, each about 5 px tall.
2. **Fix the slow-motion feel directly.** Pong's logic runs once per drawn frame, so at 7 fps it plays at about a quarter of upstream's speed. A wrapper could run the cheap game logic about 3 times per rendered frame, so the ball moves like Pong and only the picture updates at about 7 fps. I'd measure that, as it changes what you see.
3. **Cut the signal passes.** That needs a deeper patch and would reduce the noise look, so I'd leave it unless you want it.

**What I'd like from you:** please look at `c` on the board (I'd flash it pinned) and tell me if the 330 px view and half vertical resolution look acceptable. If they do, I'd make `c` the default.

Rod, step 3 measured at 8.0 fps, a smaller gain than I predicted.

| Variant | fps | step | push | rows | My prediction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `s2` (current default) | 7.2 | 124.2 ms | 15.1 ms | 330 | 7.2 fps (as measured before) |
| `s3` | **8.0** | **111.3 ms** | 15.1 ms | 330 | about 8.5 fps, about 100 ms |

Both ran 7 steady windows with no canary or reboot. Step 3 saved 12.9 ms against the 25 ms I guessed, so it's +11% fps for a third of the vertical resolution. The board currently holds `s3`, because `ab_flash` leaves the last variant flashed.

**What this says about where the time is.** Taking step 1 to 2 saved 40 ms and 2 to 3 saved another 13 ms, so the line loop at step 3 is only about 27 ms. That leaves about 84 ms of the 111 ms in the signal passes (the noise and ghost synthesis over 239k samples), plus about 13 ms of floor and about 7 ms of put. More line stepping now buys very little (step 4 would save about 7 ms). Getting past 8 fps means changing the signal passes. That is a bigger patch, and it would touch the noise look that you said looks good.

**Please look at the board now (`s3`) and tell me if 3-line steps look acceptable.** The only visible cost should be coarser vertical detail on the paddle edges and net dashes.
- **If it looks fine:** I'd make step 3 the default (8.0 fps).
- **If not:** I'd keep step 2 (7.2 fps).

**What I'd do next, my recommendation:**
1. **Game speed.** The slow-motion feel is a pacing issue: the game logic runs once per drawn frame, so at 8 fps it plays at about a quarter of Pong's 30 Hz pace. Running the cheap logic about 3 times per drawn frame would move the ball and paddles at natural speed, with the picture still updating 8 times a second. That is a bigger improvement to how it plays than a further 1 fps.
2. **Finish the port.** Pin the frame hash, record the numbers in `tools/assessment_measured.md.in` and `.claude/rules/hacks.md`, file the stack and signal-pass ideas as issues, and open the draft trail.

**Why I think the noise generator itself is cheap.** Per sample it's a multiply-add and an int-to-float conversion, about 12 cycles, so roughly 25 ms of plain compute across the 239k samples. Only skipping passes would help, and that risks the vertical sync.

**Proposed measurement, about 12 minutes, four flashes** (each 45 s, step 3, the 330 px view, built from the committed tree plus the temporary switches):

| Variant | What it does | What it isolates |

| `n` | `add_signal` skipped (the picture signal and ghost) | the cost of adding the picture |
| `mn` | both | the floor of the passes: memset plus the subtotals |

**My predictions**
- **`m`:** about 100 ms (the generator is worth about 10 ms).
- **`n`:** about 85 ms.
- **`mn`:** about 70 ms.

- **Total:** `mn`'s 10.0 fps is the ceiling for the signal side, with a blank picture. A real picture can't reach it, so 8.0 fps at step 3 is about where this design lands.

Doing the game-speed change: run Pong's cheap game logic several times per rendered frame, so the ball and paddles move at a natural pace while the picture still updates about 7 times a second.

**Design (a wrapper, no edits to `pong.c`):**
- **Skipped ticks:** `pong_draw` runs as normal (erase, move, paint into the signal) but `analogtv_draw`, the 100+ ms part, is skipped on all but every Nth call.
- **Delay:** a skipped tick returns delay 0, so the ticks run back to back instead of each waiting out 33 ms.
- **Knob:** `PONG_TICKS`, also a runtime variable for tests.

"""Mutation check for the Pong game pacing. Run with python3 -I."""

import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

WT = Path("/Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/worktrees/pong")
FW = WT / "firmware"
PIO = WT / ".venv" / "bin" / "pio"
ENV = {
    "PATH": "/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin:/opt/homebrew/bin",
    "HOME": "/Users/rod",
    "PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR": str(WT / ".platformio"),
    "NO_COLOR": "1",
}
WRAP = "firmware/src/hacks/pong_tv.c"
MUTANTS = [
    ("renders every call", "pong_drew = ++pong_tick >= pong_ticks;",
     "pong_drew = 1; ++pong_tick;"),
    ("never renders", "pong_drew = ++pong_tick >= pong_ticks;",
     "pong_drew = ++pong_tick >= 1000000;"),
    ("a skipped call keeps the pause", "return pong_drew ? delay : 0;", "return delay;"),
    ("a drawn call asks for no wait", "return pong_drew ? delay : 0;", "return 0;"),
    ("first call does not draw", "  pong_tick = pong_ticks - 1; /* the first call draws */\n", ""),
    ("counter never resets", "  pong_tick = 0;\n  analogtv_draw(it, noiselevel, recs, rec_count);",
     "  analogtv_draw(it, noiselevel, recs, rec_count);"),
    ("draws every other call whatever N is", "pong_drew = ++pong_tick >= pong_ticks;",
     "pong_drew = ++pong_tick >= 2;"),
]


def run() -> tuple[int, str]:
    p = subprocess.run(
        [str(PIO), "test", "-e", "native", "-f", "test_pong_wrapper"],
        cwd=FW, env=ENV, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=900,
    )
    out = p.stdout + p.stderr
    summary = [l for l in out.splitlines() if "test cases" in l]
    return p.returncode, (summary[-1] if summary else "no summary")


def main() -> int:
    rc, s = run()
    print(f"BASELINE: rc={rc} {s}", flush=True)
    if rc != 0:
        return 1
    path = WT / WRAP
    for name, old, new in MUTANTS:
        original = path.read_text()
        if original.count(old) != 1:
            print(f"SKIPPED (count {original.count(old)}): {name}", flush=True)
            continue
        try:
            path.write_text(original.replace(old, new))
            rc, s = run()
        finally:
            path.write_text(original)
        print(("killed" if rc != 0 else "SURVIVED") + f": {name} ({s})", flush=True)
    return 0


sys.exit(main())

Rod, the sped-up build is on the board and running. Please have a look.

**Measured over 60 s, no canary or reboot.** The log's `fps` now counts game steps a second, not pictures, since the wrapper calls the game every step and draws every third.

| | Before (step 3) | Now (3 game steps per picture) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| game steps a second | 8.0 | **22.2** |
| pictures a second | 8.0 | about 7.4 |
| average step | 111 ms | 38.6 ms |
| game pace against upstream's 30 Hz | 27% | **74%** |

- **Skipped steps are cheap:** about 2.5 ms each. The average works out as one drawn step of about 111 ms plus two skipped steps, divided by three, and the capture matches that.
- **The picture updates a touch slower:** about 7.4 a second against 8.0, because the skipped steps take a little time.
- **Pace is tunable:** because skipped steps cost so little, 4 per picture should reach about 96% of upstream's pace at about 7.2 pictures a second, and 5 would overshoot to about 115%. That's my arithmetic from these numbers, not a measurement.
- **The trade-off:** the ball jumps further between pictures, about 4 game steps at a time, so motion can look choppier even though the game moves at the right speed. The ball is 16 px wide and moves about 6 px a step.

Please tell me if the motion now looks like Pong or like jumping. If you want a different ratio, I can flash 2, 4 or 5 and we can compare. The ratio changes the frames, so I'll pin the frame hash only after you've chosen.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/skills/deliver-branch

# Delivering a branch

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `entire trail create --title ... --type feature --body ...` pushes the branch
  (`--type` takes only `bug`, `feature` or `task`; `chore` is refused)
  and opens a linked DRAFT PR. The PR body is not synced from the trail: update
  both (`entire trail update --body`, `gh pr edit N --body-file`). Put
  `Fixes #N` in the body, then read the PR back (`gh pr view N --json body`):
  #27 merged with the generic body, so `Fixes #23` never reached GitHub and
  the issue stayed open until it was closed by hand.
- Rod approves and merges (merge commit). Afterwards delete the merged branch
  (remote and local) without asking and fast-forward `main`. Confirm the merge
  after a fresh `git fetch`: a stale `origin/main` says "not merged". Remove
  the branch's worktree first (a checked-out branch cannot be deleted), and
  note that `git branch -d` refuses while local `main` is behind, so check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main` and then use `-D`. `main` is
  usually checked out in Rod's main checkout, so `git fetch origin main:main`
  is refused there: run `git merge --ff-only origin/main` in it, only if
  `git status` shows no tracked changes.
- Merge with `gh pr ready N` then `entire trail merge <trail>` (the trail
  number, not the PR number; omit it on the trail's branch) once Rod approves
  (trail PRs are drafts). `entire trail merge` checks the gates first and
  merges nothing while one fails or is pending; `--dry-run` reports which.
  Rod's approval is enough: do not wait for the Entire Gates check to finish.
  If the only failing gates are Approvals (he approved in chat) or a stacked
  PR's "Up to date: 1 commit behind" once its parent merges, and the PR is
  mergeable, try `entire trail merge <trail> --force --yes` with no rebase;
  the bypass is recorded on the trail. The repo's bypass policy is now
  "nobody", so it is refused ("does not allow bypassing gates", PR #132):
  do not merge round it with `gh pr merge`. Ask Rod to approve the trail in
  the Entire UI, then run a plain `entire trail merge`. For any other failing
  gate, stop and tell Rod.
- Before merging, `git fetch` and compare the PR's `headRefOid` with your tip:
  Rod sometimes pushes to the branch (docs commits, a merge of `main`). Read
  what arrived with `git log --oneline <tip>..origin/<branch>`, and clean up
  from the merge commit, not your last push. After `ExitWorktree keep` the
  tool names the branch `worktree-<name>`; the real branch is
  `git worktree list`'s.
- A trail's "N commits behind" can understate: trail 66 said 1 and its branch
  was 17 behind. Count with `git rev-list --count <branch>..origin/main`
  before a cherry-pick, and re-apply by hand if the files conflict.
- To read another agent's session, run `entire checkpoint explain <checkpoint>
  --full` (or `--transcript` for the JSONL) from the repo root: elsewhere it
  says "not a git repository". `entire session info <id>` knows only local
  sessions, so find the checkpoint with `entire checkpoint explain <sha>` on
  one of the agent's commits.
- A review of fixed code can raise a new finding on the fix itself (a clamp
  that did not stop a wrap). Reproduce it with a failing test before changing
  the code, and mutation-check each branch of the new guard.
- Write a PR body to a file for `gh pr edit --body-file` (an apostrophe in an
  inline `--body '...'` must be `'"'"'`).
- `gh pr edit N --body-file` replaces the whole body, including the
  `<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->` ... `-end -->` block at the top. Keep that
  block in the file, or the PR loses its trail.
- Findings: `entire trail finding list N`, then `... resolve N <id> -m "..."`.
  Bot reviews can lag about 20 minutes. `N` is the trail number (PR #12 was
  trail 6), not the PR number. For a false positive or upstream behaviour in a
  byte-identical hack, use `entire trail finding dismiss N <id> -m "<reason>"`.
- To file your own review's findings: `entire trail finding add --trail N
  --client-id <key> --severity high|medium|low --file <path> --start-line A
  --end-line B -m "<body>"` (no title flag; the client id makes a re-run safe).
  Open the body by saying an agent filed it for Rod.
- In a worktree session create the trail with a one-line `--body`, then set the
  real body with `gh pr edit N --body-file` (keep the trail-link block), and
  check `closingIssuesReferences` with `gh pr view N --json` (it can lag a
  few seconds).
- `entire trail update --body` takes no number and acts on the current
  branch (`entire trail update 8` errors).
- Stacked PR: `entire trail create --base <parent-branch>`. When the parent
  merges, `gh pr edit N --base main` before deleting its branch, then
  `git rebase --onto origin/main <old parent tip>`. The rebased push needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod first), unless the branch was never pushed.
- `docs/porting-assessment.md` conflicts on rebase: `git checkout --theirs`
  it to continue, then rerun `tools/score_hacks.py` and amend the result in.
- Two ports in flight both append to `g_hacks[]`, so whichever merges second
  conflicts in `registry.c`, the expected list in `test_hacks.c`,
  `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, `tools/assessment_measured.md.in` (rows,
  paragraphs and the hack count) and the three `build_src_filter` lines in `platformio.ini`,
  as well as the generated assessment. Keep both sides, put the newer hack
  last, and regenerate the assessment. A rebased published branch needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod), and GitHub can reject that push once too.
- A finding that says the code "does not exist" can be stale after a rebase
  (the skill PR was reviewed before the Blaster and Substrate code it referred
  to had landed). Check it against `main` before dismissing, and put the
  evidence in the dismissal. Entire's approvals gate once showed "no reviewers
  have approved" right after a force push, though Rod had approved; his word is
  enough, so say so and go ahead.
- `entire trail finding list` can show one open "Review verdict ... approve"
  finding: it is the reviewers' verdict, not a defect. `mergeStateStatus`
  reads UNSTABLE while the gate runs, and Rod's approval is enough.
- A shared-code PR (stroker, runner, canvas) can move pins of hacks merged
  since it branched: merge or rebase onto `main` and rerun the pin loop before
  judging frames (Celtic joined #89's moved set after #88 landed).
- Why a gate is red: `gh api
  repos/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/commits/<branch>/check-runs
  --jq '.check_runs[]|.output.summary'`.
  "Approvals: failed" is just Rod not having approved yet, and "Checks:
  skipped" is normal (no CI here). `entire trail watch` streams forever, so to
  watch poll `gh pr view N`, that API and `entire trail finding list N` from a
  script file under a Monitor, printing only on change. Merge only when Rod
  says to, even once the gates are green.
- If `entire trail create` reports "failed to push branch", run
  `git push -u origin <branch>` and rerun it: the trail is then created.
- Run `gh pr ready N` and `entire trail merge <trail>` as separate commands:
  on a PR that is already ready, `ready` exits non-zero and skips a chained
  merge.
  Confirm with `gh pr view N --json state`.
- `entire trail merge <trail> --dry-run` can say "findings pending: Waiting
  for the agent review of the current head" with "bypass policy (nobody)".
  Rod merging `main` into the branch makes a new head and the review runs
  again (it cleared in under 20 minutes). `--force` is refused: poll the dry
  run from a script under a Monitor, then merge when it reads "Mergeable:
  yes". First `git fetch`, compare the PR's `headRefOid` with the tip, and
  check `finding list --status open`.

## Linear: creating the trail

After Rod approves creating it, do all three steps together:

1. Start the trail body with `Linear: ARS-NN` and the ticket URL, so a
   reader of the trail can reach the ticket.
1. Run `entire trail create`, then comment the trail URL on the ticket.
1. Set the ticket to **In Review**.

If a draft trail already exists for the work, link it in the new trail's
body. A draft trail has no branch and cannot be attached to one, so the
new trail supersedes it; tell Rod so he can close the draft.

## Linear: after the merge

When Rod says the trail is approved: run `entire trail merge N --dry-run`,
merge it, fast-forward local `main`, and delete the merged branch locally
and on origin. Then set the ticket to **Done**. If the merge fails or Rod
asks for changes, set the ticket back to **In Progress**.

Linear: [ARS-59](https://linear.app/arsecandle/issue/ARS-59/port-pong-xscreensaver-via-analogtv)

## What this adds

Pong, the first hack that runs through xscreensaver's `analogtv` (a software
model of a CRT picture: signal, noise, ghosting, scanlines). `pong.c`,
`analogtv.c` and `analogtv.h` are byte-identical to `vendor/xscreensaver-6.17`
(`cmp`-checked). Everything else is a wrapper, a build-time patch or a shim
addition.

## How it gets to a usable speed

As copied it ran at 2.8 fps. Each step below was measured on the board.

| Build | Pictures a second | Step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| As copied | 2.8 | 356 ms |
| `float` ghost filter | 4.6 | 194.6 ms |
| Draw every 3rd line, 330 px view | 8.0 | 111.3 ms |
| Registered (3 game steps for each picture) | about 7.4 pictures, 22.2 game steps a second | 38.6 ms mean per call |

- **Float ghost filter** (`tools/analogtv_patch.py`, run by
  `firmware/patch_analogtv.py` on a build-directory copy). The filter taps are
  `double`, which the ESP32-S3 does in software: 209 of the 356 ms. A C test
  compares the patched function with the real one.
- **Line step 3.** The picture's line loop draws every 3rd line over the rows
  of the lines it skips.
- **330 px view.** The largest square inside the round glass, so the bezel no
  longer cuts the paddles.
- **Noise 0.02** (upstream 0.04), which Rod preferred.
- **Game pacing.** The picture is about 111 ms and a game step almost nothing,
  so the picture is drawn on every 3rd call and the others return a delay of
  0. The game runs at about 74% of upstream's pace. The ball moves about four
  game steps between pictures.
- Knobs (compile-time, `ab_flash`-able): `PONG_LINE_STEP`, `PONG_VIEW`,
  `PONG_NOISE`, `PONG_TICKS`. Step 1, noise 0.04 and the whole window
  reproduce the original frames byte for byte on the host.

## Shim additions

Test-first in `test_xshim`: pointer and cursor no-ops, `XHeightOfScreen`,
`XQueryColors`, the visual's class and RGB masks, 1-bit `XYPixmap` images,
`thread_malloc`/`thread_free`, and a few headers.

## Verification

- **Host:** full native suite 944/944, `pytest tools/tests` 688 passed and 1
  skipped, `check_notices.py` clean, pre-commit passed. Mutation checks: 15
  shim mutants, 7 pacing mutants and 14 line step and view mutants killed.
  Two survivors are equivalent (the `lineno + k < ANALOGTV_BOT` guard; "always
  overlaps", which is true at the whole-window default).
- **Device:** flashed and run on the board. Rod looked at it and said it
  looks great. Measured: no stack canary or reboot over a 60 s capture;
  stack free minimum 2.8 KB of 16 KB as copied (analogtv's 9.3 KB `yiq`
  array), not re-measured on the final build.
- The frame hash is pinned from the build Rod looked at.
- `ty` was skipped on the commits (`SKIP=ty`): the worktree's shared `.venv`
  has no `ty`.

## Not done

- Stack headroom (2.8 KB) is thin; a mitigation is a possible follow-up.
- Other `analogtv` hacks (xanalogtv, apple2 and so on) are untried.

input.project_notes: Pong port (ARS-59, trail 91): analogtv at 2.8 fps as copied. 209 of 356 ms was double-precision ghost taps (soft-double on S3); a build-time float patch of analogtv.c keeps the vendor copy byte-identical. Line step 3 + 330px view gave 8 pictures/s, which is about the ceiling: ~38 ms is PSRAM traffic on the 955 KB signal buffer, found by skipping stages one at a time. Skipped lines must be blasted at their own height; extending ybot made dark bands because analogtv's level table is only built near average height. Because the picture costs ~111 ms and a game step ~nothing, drawing every 3rd call and returning delay 0 otherwise took game pace from 27% to 74% of upstream's.
input.technical_insights: When a hack's cost is nearly all rendering, decouple simulation ticks from picture draws instead of speeding up the render. Measure by skipping stages (experiments), not guessing; pacing numbers per call mean something different from per-picture numbers, so say which.
input.user_context: Rod judged by eye on the board: said the 4.6 fps build looked like slow motion, then "Looks great" to the paced build. He wants noise dialled back. He gave go-ahead to run tests and open the trail in one message.

input.content: 📺 Ported Pong to a 466px round AMOLED through xscreensaver's analogtv CRT emulator. 2.8 fps as copied 🐌 → the culprit was double-precision ghost taps (209 of 356 ms) in soft-float on the ESP32-S3. A build-time float patch kept the vendor file byte-identical. Then the neat trick: the picture costs ~111 ms but a game step costs ~nothing, so draw every 3rd call and let the game run 3x faster 🏓 Game pace 27% → 74% of upstream. Lesson: decouple simulation from rendering before trying to speed up rendering. Skipping stages one at a time showed the real floor (PSRAM traffic) 🔬

Pong is merged (PR #149, `0373307`) and ARS-59 is Done. I deleted the branch locally and on origin, removed the worktree and fast-forwarded `main`. The board still holds the Pong-pinned build.

Seven files in the vendored `hacks/` directory use `analogtv`. I've only grepped their dependencies, not built any of them, so this ranking is a first guess.

| Hack | What it is | Obstacles | My guess |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `xanalogtv` | Cycles fake TV channels: logo, test patterns, static, loaded images | `ximage-loader` and `load_image` (7 `XGetImage` calls, probably grabbing the screen). `XrmDatabase`/`XrmPutResource` also show up in the scorer's gap list. | Best next port. We already have the image-grab pieces from Truchet and the Win95 grab. |
| `filmleader` | Countdown film leader with a sweep arm and Xft text | 23 Xft calls. The XJack Xft stand-in should mostly cover it. | Second pick. Mostly large type and simple shapes. |
| `vfeedback` | Video feedback: feeds its own picture back into the TV | `analogtv_load_ximage` and `XGetImage` every frame, on top of the picture cost. | Probably too slow to bother with. |
| `apple2-main` (with `m6502`) | An Apple ][ terminal and 6502 emulator | `popen`/`fork` and a `textclient` that runs a real process. | Possible if we replace the process with a canned session, as we did for Phosphor. Real work, since `m6502` is a CPU emulator. |
| `bsod` | Fake crash screens, one of them Apple ][ | `fork`, `popen`, 36 Xft calls, and most of its screens don't use `analogtv`. | Biggest and hardest. Last. |

Every one of these pays the same cost as Pong: about 111 ms for a picture, so roughly 8 pictures a second. That suits `xanalogtv` and `filmleader`, where slow channel changes and a countdown don't need more. The terminal-style hacks would look jerky.

I'd do `xanalogtv` first, then `filmleader`. The scorer rows are stale: they list gaps Pong already filled, so `score_hacks.py` will show the real gaps once it's re-run. I haven't filed any Linear tickets. Want me to open one for `xanalogtv` and start?
Yes, file the ticket and start on xanalogtv and filmleaders as a batch.  You can flash the device as you work on them.

"""Turn an image into the C header that Maze's logo is read from.

The device has no PNG decoder, so the image goes in as a raw RGB565 blob with
a 1-bit mask. The layout is documented in
firmware/src/x11shim/include/ximage-loader.h.

Run with: uv run tools/make_logo_blob.py logo-50.gif --name logo_50_png \\
    -o firmware/src/x11shim/include/images/gen/logo-50_png.h
"""

import argparse
import sys
import zlib
from pathlib import Path

OPAQUE_ALPHA = 128


def rgb565(r: int, g: int, b: int) -> int:
    return (r & 0xF8) << 8 | (g & 0xFC) << 3 | b >> 3


def build_blob(width: int, height: int, rgba: bytes) -> bytes:
    if not (0 < width <= 0xFFFF and 0 < height <= 0xFFFF):
        raise ValueError(f"size {width}x{height} does not fit the blob header")
    if len(rgba) != width * height * 4:
        raise ValueError(f"expected {width * height * 4} RGBA bytes, got {len(rgba)}")

    pixels = bytearray()
    mask = bytearray()
    stride = (width + 7) // 8
    for y in range(height):
        row = bytearray(stride)
        for x in range(width):
            r, g, b, a = rgba[(y * width + x) * 4 :][:4]
            opaque = a >= OPAQUE_ALPHA

#ifndef ANALOGTV_TV_H
#define ANALOGTV_TV_H

/* What the shared analogtv build (analogtv_tv.c) reads when it draws. A hack that
 * uses analogtv sets these in its init, since the last one to start leaves its
 * values behind; the defaults are upstream's. */

a graph sized to the screen. The first function's notes come first.

spline_value_at picks a segment with `si = floor(t*n)` and then the position in

precision that holds. In float the compiler fuses the second multiply and the
subtraction (the S3's `madd.s`, and arm64 on the host), so `tt` uses the exact
product while `si` came from the product rounded to a float: t = 0.331093 with
3422 segments rounds to exactly 1133 and gives tt = -1.4e-5, and the abort
stopped the board.

The copied celtic.c stays byte-identical to upstream. The firmware build runs
this on its text before the float literal pass (firmware/patch_float_literals.py).

"""Build-time patch for FilmLeader: a square canvas of a size we choose.

Upstream draws the leader into a pixmap 712 pixels wide and 16:9, and analogtv
stretches it over the window. On the round 466 by 466 panel that squashes the
rings into upright ovals, and the pixmap (712 by 712, since it is sized for
the longer side) and the image `XGetImage` makes from it each frame are 1 MB
and 2 MB. The copied filmleader.c stays byte-identical: the firmware build runs
this on its text (firmware/patch_analogtv.py), and src/hacks/filmleader_tv.c
includes the result.

The aspect ratio becomes 1, and the width becomes `FILMLEADER_CANVAS`, which
the wrapper defines. The font sizes upstream asks for are in canvas pixels, so
the wrapper scales them with the canvas.

Each replacement is checked, so a change upstream fails the build loudly.
"""

OLD_ASPECT = "    double r = 16/9.0;\n"
NEW_ASPECT = "    double r = 1.0;\n"

OLD_WIDTH = "    st->w = 712;\n"
NEW_WIDTH = "    st->w = FILMLEADER_CANVAS;\n"


def _replace_once(source: str, old: str, new: str, what: str) -> str:
    found = source.count(old)
    if found != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"expected 1 {what} in filmleader.c, found {found}; has upstream changed?"
        )
    return source.replace(old, new)


def square_canvas(source: str) -> str:
    source = _replace_once(source, OLD_ASPECT, NEW_ASPECT, "16:9 aspect ratio")
    return _replace_once(source, OLD_WIDTH, NEW_WIDTH, "712 pixel canvas width")

def c_bytes(data: bytes) -> str:
    rows = []
    for i in range(0, len(data), 24):
        rows.append("  " + ",".join(f"{b}" for b in data[i : i + 24]) + ",")
    return "\n".join(rows)


def c_header(name: str, font: list[dict], source: str) -> str:
    guard = f"GENERATED_{name.upper()}_H"
    out = [
        f"/* Generated by tools/make_font_atlas.py from {source}. Do not edit. */",
        f"#ifndef {guard}",
        f"#define {guard}",
        '#include "x11shim/xft_font.h"',
        "",
    ]
    for size in font:
        px = size["pixel_size"]
        out.append(f"static const unsigned char {name}_alpha_{px}[] = {{")
        out.append(c_bytes(size["alpha"]) if size["alpha"] else "  0,")
        out.append("};")
        out.append(f"static const XshimGlyph {name}_glyphs_{px}[] = {{")
        for g in size["glyphs"]:
            out.append(
                f"  {{{g['w']},{g['h']},{g['left']},{g['top']},"
                f"{g['advance']},{g['offset']}}},"
            )
        out.append("};")
    out.append(f"static const XshimFontSize {name}_sizes[] = {{")
    for size in font:
        px = size["pixel_size"]
        out.append(
            f"  {{{px},{size['ascent']},{size['descent']},"
            f"{name}_glyphs_{px},{name}_alpha_{px}}},"
        )
    out.append("};")
    out.append(f"static const XshimFont {name}_font = {{{len(font)}, {name}_sizes}};")
    out.append(f"#endif /* {guard} */")
    return "\n".join(out) + "\n"


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=(__doc__ or "").split("\n\n")[0])
    parser.add_argument("ttf", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("--name", required=True, help="C identifier prefix")
    parser.add_argument("--sizes", required=True, help="comma-separated pixel sizes")
    parser.add_argument("-o", "--output", type=Path, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    try:
        sizes = sorted({int(s) for s in args.sizes.split(",")})
        font = build_font(args.ttf, sizes)
    except ValueError as err:
        print(f"make_font_atlas: {err}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    args.output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    args.output.write_text(c_header(args.name, font, args.ttf.name))
    return 0

Most of that is `analogtv_load_ximage`, now about 250 ms of it, plus 111 ms for the picture and about 150 ms for its own drawing. Rod, an update on ARS-60 (XAnalogTV and FilmLeader). Both now run on the board with no reboots, and the work is committed on `feature/ARS-60-xanalogtv-filmleader`.

**On the board**
- **XAnalogTV:** about 7.2 pictures a second, step ~123 ms, PSRAM steady.
- **FilmLeader:** about 2.0 pictures a second, step ~515 ms. It's slow because it loads a fresh picture every frame, about 250 ms of that step. I'm not sure that's good enough for a countdown, so I'd like you to look at it.

**What went wrong on the way**
- **Stack overflow:** `analogtv_load_ximage` keeps 28 KB of colour rows on the stack, so XAnalogTV boot-looped. A build-time patch now reads each sample where it's used. The patch's output is compared with the real function under AddressSanitizer.
- **Out of PSRAM:** the three test cards, held as 32-bit images, left too little for the first load. They're freed once setup finishes.
- **FilmLeader bugs found by the tests:** a one-byte over-read in the upstream source, which AddressSanitizer caught, and three fonts that upstream's free never closes. Both are patched and tested.

**One shared change to flag:** `XQueryColor` now uses a table instead of three divides. Every one of the 65,536 pixel values is checked against the old formula, so output is the same, but every hack that calls it sees the new code.

**Still pending:** the final full native suite is running in the background. The previous run had one failure, the FilmLeader leak, which is now fixed. Then the docs, measurements and trail.

**Test cards:** they come from xscreensaver's own images, whose licence isn't stated. I kept them out of git and convert them from `vendor/` at build time, and there's a notices section for them.

**Please look at the screen.** The board currently shows FilmLeader, pinned and with rotation off. Two questions:
- **FilmLeader:** it runs at about 2 pictures a second (step ~515 ms). Is that acceptable for a countdown? There are two ways to improve it: half the canvas rows, or dropping to a single line step. Both would look softer.
- **XAnalogTV:** it runs at about 7.2 pictures a second and is mostly TV snow. That's upstream's behaviour, since most channels are weak stations, and colour bars and test cards come up now and then. I can flash it so you can judge.

**To open the trail** I need your approval. The new hacks aren't pinned in `test_hacks`, because their pictures follow the wall clock. I haven't measured stack headroom on either hack.

**1. Full screen: yes, it's one flag each, but it costs speed.**

- **How:** `-DXANALOGTV_VIEW=0` and `-DFILMLEADER_VIEW=0` make the picture cover the whole 466 px window. They are currently 330, the biggest square that fits inside the round glass. The corners of a full-window picture sit behind the bezel, so about a fifth of the extra pixels are never seen.
- **Cost:** the drawing and push work goes up by about 2× (466² against 330²), and the push becomes a full 24.8 ms frame. Part of each step doesn't shrink with the view, so I'd expect something like 5–6 fps for XAnalogTV (now ~7) and about 1.4 for FilmLeader (now ~2). Those figures are my estimate, not measured.
- **Compensating:** raising the line step from 3 to 4 would win some speed back, at the price of a softer picture.

**2. Interference: turning it down won't help.**

- **No saving from a lower level:** in `analogtv_init_signal`, the level only scales one multiplier (`noisemul`). The loop still generates a random number for every sample, and the ghost-filter taps in `analogtv_add_signal` run on every sample whatever the level.
- **Not the whole cost either:** the work is the signal pass (noise, ghosting and sums over every sample), then demodulating each line, then writing the pixels. The pixel writing is the part that shrinks with a smaller view or a bigger line step. The signal pass doesn't, and "redrawing the whole screen" is only part of the step.
- **What I haven't measured:** how much of the ~123 ms step is the random-number loop. If I cut it out in the build-time patch, I'd guess it saves a modest slice, because it's one multiply and add per sample, but I don't know. It would also remove the snow that makes the picture look like a TV.

I can run the measurement on the board. It would be an A/B of XAnalogTV at the current settings, full-screen at step 3, full-screen at step 4, and the noise loop removed. That means flashing builds over the FilmLeader you're looking at. Shall I go ahead?
Yes, flash them and measure. And try increasign the line step too and see what that does for the numbers

The line-step and full-screen numbers are in. My first no-noise build did nothing, so I'm re-running that comparison with a proper build-time edit and will report when it's done.

Board results for XAnalogTV (2 rounds each, 60 s windows, rotation off). The two rounds agreed to within 0.01 fps:

| Variant | fps | step | push | rows |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Current: 330 view, step 3 | 7.31 | 122.8 ms | 15.1 ms | 330 |
| 330 view, step 4 | 7.84 | 113.3 ms | 15.1 ms | 330 |
| Full screen, step 3 | 6.60 | 152.4 ms | 0.1 ms | 466 |
| Full screen, step 4 | 7.10 | 142.1 ms | 0.1 ms | 466 |
| Full screen, step 6 | 7.68 | 131.3 ms | 0.1 ms | 466 |

- **Full screen costs little:** step 3 at full screen is only about 10% slower than now (6.60 against 7.31 fps). That's much better than the 2× I guessed.
- **Why:** a full-screen picture lets the push overlap the next step (the `repaints_all` flag), so the 15 ms push disappears into the step.
- **Line step gains are small:** each extra line of step buys about 0.4 fps at full screen (3→4 is +0.5 fps, 4→6 is +0.6 fps). Most of the step is fixed per frame, so a coarser picture doesn't buy much.
- **My pick:** full screen at step 4 (7.1 fps, about the same speed as now). Step 6 gets 7.7 fps, but I'd expect it to look noticeably coarse.
OK, let's default to full screen at step 4.  And unregister filmleader.  It's not worth trying to save.
